questions.stem: A client presents with sudden onset of unilateral facial drooping, inability to close one eye, and loss of the nasolabial fold on the affected side, with no other neurological deficits, and a family member insists this must automatically mean a stroke is occurring. The nurse should recognize this presentation as potentially consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A normal variant of facial movement requiring no further clinical evaluation, contrary to what this concerning presentation actually warrants","B":"An unrelated dermatological skin condition with no connection to facial nerve function, which does not fit this particular presentation","C":"Bell's palsy, a peripheral facial nerve condition, though stroke must still be carefully ruled out given the overlapping initial presentation, rather than automatically assuming stroke as the family member insists","D":"A stroke, requiring the identical emergency workup regardless of any other clinical findings present, similar to what the family member is currently insisting"}}
questions.rationale: Bell's palsy is an idiopathic peripheral facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) paralysis causing unilateral facial drooping, inability to close the eye, and loss of the nasolabial fold. However, because its initial presentation can overlap with stroke, careful neurological assessment is essential to rule out central causes (such as forehead sparing, which is more typical of central/stroke-related facial weakness) before confirming a Bell's palsy diagnosis.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Neurology — Bell's Palsy Clinical Guideline
questions.source_detail: Clinical Presentation and Differentiation from Stroke

questions.stem: A client reports sudden, severe, brief episodes of stabbing facial pain triggered by activities such as chewing, talking, or light touch to the face, and initially assumes this must be a dental problem needing a dentist visit. The nurse should recognize this as potentially consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A normal dental issue requiring no further neurological evaluation, similar to what the client is currently assuming about their own symptoms","B":"Trigeminal neuralgia, rather than the dental problem the client initially assumed given this particular pattern of triggered facial pain","C":"A migraine headache, a diagnosis that would not typically produce this specific pattern of brief, trigger-related facial pain","D":"An unrelated ear infection, which would not explain this particular pattern of triggered, brief stabbing facial pain"}}
questions.rationale: Trigeminal neuralgia is characterized by sudden, severe, brief episodes of stabbing or electric shock-like facial pain along the distribution of the trigeminal nerve, often triggered by routine activities such as chewing, talking, or light touch, distinct from the more prolonged, throbbing pain typical of migraine.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Neurology — Trigeminal Neuralgia Clinical Presentation
questions.source_detail: Characteristic Pain Pattern of Trigeminal Neuralgia

questions.stem: A client reports an uncomfortable, uncontrollable urge to move the legs, particularly in the evening or at rest, which is relieved by movement, and a family member assumes this is simply a sign of poor circulation from sitting too much. The nurse should recognize this as potentially consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Peripheral artery disease exclusively, a condition typically presenting with exertional pain rather than the urge-to-move pattern described here","B":"Restless leg syndrome, rather than the poor circulation the family member is currently assuming, given this specific evening and rest-related pattern","C":"An unrelated psychiatric condition, which would not explain this particular physical urge-to-move pattern being described","D":"A normal finding requiring no further evaluation, similar to what the family member is currently assuming about this symptom pattern"}}
questions.rationale: Restless leg syndrome is characterized by an uncomfortable, uncontrollable urge to move the legs, typically worsening in the evening or during periods of rest/inactivity, and temporarily relieved by movement, distinct from vascular conditions like peripheral artery disease, which is more associated with pain during activity.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Sleep Medicine — Restless Leg Syndrome Diagnostic Criteria
questions.source_detail: Clinical Presentation of Restless Leg Syndrome

questions.stem: A client with severe lower back pain develops new saddle anesthesia (numbness in the perineal/buttock area), bilateral leg weakness, and new bowel/bladder dysfunction. The nurse should recognize this as a possible sign of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A urinary tract infection with no accompanying spinal cord or nerve involvement present","B":"Cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency requiring immediate evaluation and intervention","C":"Simple sciatica requiring only conservative, non-urgent management of the client's symptoms","D":"A normal disc-related pain pattern requiring only routine, non-urgent outpatient follow-up"}}
questions.rationale: Saddle anesthesia, bilateral leg weakness, and new bowel/bladder dysfunction in the context of severe back pain are red flag symptoms of cauda equina syndrome, a surgical emergency caused by compression of the cauda equina nerve roots, requiring immediate evaluation (MRI) and often emergency surgical decompression to prevent permanent neurological damage.
questions.source_name: North American Spine Society — Cauda Equina Syndrome Red Flags
questions.source_detail: Recognition of Cauda Equina Syndrome as a Surgical Emergency

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a client's prealbumin level as part of a nutritional assessment after a recent dietary change, and a colleague assumes checking albumin alone would have given the same up-to-date information. Compared with albumin, prealbumin is instead considered:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Identical in overall clinical usefulness to albumin, with no meaningfully distinguishing features, similar to what the colleague is currently assuming","B":"A less clinically useful nutritional marker with no genuine value in this kind of assessment, contrary to why prealbumin is actually being checked here","C":"Only relevant for assessing the client's current kidney function, not nutritional status, which does not describe what prealbumin is actually used for","D":"A more sensitive short-term marker of nutritional status, due to its shorter half-life, addressing why it can reflect recent changes better than albumin as the colleague assumed"}}
questions.rationale: Prealbumin has a much shorter half-life (about 2 days) compared to albumin (about 20 days), making it a more sensitive marker for detecting short-term changes in nutritional status and response to nutritional interventions, though it can also be affected by inflammation and other factors requiring careful interpretation.
questions.source_name: ASPEN — Nutritional Assessment Biomarkers
questions.source_detail: Prealbumin as a Short-Term Nutritional Marker

questions.stem: A client with suspected disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) has lab work drawn, including fibrinogen. The nurse understands that in DIC, fibrinogen levels are typically:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Elevated, due to increased fibrinogen production during this particular clotting disorder","B":"Unaffected by DIC, since fibrinogen levels are not involved in this clotting disorder","C":"Decreased, since fibrinogen is consumed during the abnormal widespread clotting process characteristic of DIC","D":"Only relevant for assessing the client's platelet function, not their fibrinogen level"}}
questions.rationale: In DIC, fibrinogen (a clotting factor) is typically decreased, since it is consumed during the abnormal, widespread activation of the clotting cascade characteristic of this condition, contributing to the paradoxical bleeding risk that occurs alongside microvascular clotting.
questions.source_name: Clinical Hematology References — Fibrinogen in DIC
questions.source_detail: Decreased Fibrinogen as a DIC Laboratory Finding

questions.stem: A client's AST and ALT levels are significantly elevated above the normal range. The nurse should recognize this finding as most consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Kidney dysfunction exclusively, a finding unrelated to these particular liver enzyme values","B":"A normal finding that requires no further follow-up or additional liver evaluation","C":"Hepatocellular injury or inflammation, warranting further evaluation of liver function","D":"Normal liver function, a finding inconsistent with this significantly elevated laboratory result"}}
questions.rationale: AST and ALT are liver enzymes that are typically elevated in the setting of hepatocellular injury or inflammation (such as from hepatitis, medication toxicity, or other liver conditions), and significant elevation warrants further evaluation of liver function and the underlying cause.
questions.source_name: Clinical Laboratory Reference Standards — Liver Function Panel Interpretation
questions.source_detail: AST/ALT Elevation and Hepatocellular Injury

questions.stem: A client's free T4 level is below the normal range, along with an elevated TSH, and a new nurse assumes these two abnormal values together must point toward an overactive thyroid. The nurse should recognize this specific combination as consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A finding unrelated to thyroid function, contrary to what both of these abnormal thyroid-related values actually indicate together","B":"Primary hypothyroidism, rather than the overactive thyroid condition the new nurse is currently assuming based on these two values","C":"Normal thyroid function, despite both values actually falling outside their expected normal ranges","D":"Hyperthyroidism, contrary to what this specific low T4 combined with elevated TSH pattern actually indicates"}}
questions.rationale: A low free T4 combined with an elevated TSH is the classic laboratory pattern of primary hypothyroidism, in which the thyroid gland is underproducing thyroid hormone, prompting increased pituitary TSH secretion in an attempt to stimulate more hormone production.
questions.source_name: American Thyroid Association — Thyroid Function Test Interpretation
questions.source_detail: Free T4 and TSH Pattern in Primary Hypothyroidism

questions.stem: A client with suspected sepsis has an elevated serum lactate level, and a colleague assumes this lab value mainly reflects how well the client's kidneys happen to be filtering that day. The nurse should recognize this finding as significant because it can instead indicate:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A finding entirely unrelated to the client's current clinical status or suspected sepsis, contrary to why lactate is actually being monitored here","B":"Tissue hypoperfusion and anaerobic metabolism, which is associated with poorer outcomes in sepsis and requires prompt intervention, rather than reflecting kidney filtration as the colleague assumed","C":"Improved oxygen delivery to the tissues, a finding inconsistent with this client's actual elevated lactate level","D":"Normal cellular metabolism, a finding inconsistent with this client's significantly elevated lactate result"}}
questions.rationale: Elevated serum lactate reflects tissue hypoperfusion and a shift to anaerobic metabolism, which occurs when oxygen delivery to tissues is inadequate — a finding associated with poorer outcomes in sepsis and other critical illness, prompting prompt fluid resuscitation and other interventions per sepsis management protocols.
questions.source_name: Surviving Sepsis Campaign — Lactate as a Marker of Tissue Hypoperfusion
questions.source_detail: Clinical Significance of Elevated Lactate in Sepsis

questions.stem: A nurse is explaining the difference between an arterial blood gas (ABG) and a venous blood gas (VBG) to a nursing student, who assumes the two tests are basically interchangeable for every clinical purpose. The nurse should explain that ABG sampling instead:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Provides a more accurate assessment of oxygenation status (PaO2) specifically, since it reflects arterial (post-lung) blood, while VBG has more limited use for this particular purpose, contrary to the student's assumption that the two are interchangeable","B":"Is reserved almost exclusively for research or specialty settings, since venous sampling is generally considered adequate for routine bedside assessment of oxygenation","C":"Is comparable to venous sampling for assessing oxygenation status, with only minor practical differences, similar to what the student is currently assuming","D":"Is focused mainly on electrolyte and glucose values, with acid-base and oxygenation status typically assessed instead through separate venous testing"}}
questions.rationale: Arterial blood gas sampling reflects oxygenated, post-pulmonary blood, providing an accurate assessment of oxygenation status (PaO2) in addition to acid-base status, whereas venous blood gas primarily reflects tissue metabolism and has more limited direct use for assessing oxygenation, though it can still provide useful acid-base and some metabolic information in certain clinical contexts.
questions.source_name: Clinical Respiratory References — ABG vs. VBG Clinical Utility
questions.source_detail: Key Differences Between Arterial and Venous Blood Gas Sampling

questions.stem: A nurse needs to administer multiple crushed medications via a client's feeding tube, and a colleague in a hurry suggests just combining everything into one mixture to save time. Best practice instead includes:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Combining all of the crushed medications directly into the client's tube feeding formula, to reduce the number of separate administration steps, similar to what the colleague is suggesting","B":"Administering the crushed medications back-to-back without an interposed water flush between them, in order to save time, similar to what the colleague is suggesting","C":"Administering each medication separately, flushing the tube with water between medications, to prevent drug interactions within the tube and ensure the tube remains patent, rather than combining everything as the colleague suggested","D":"Crushing and combining every ordered medication into a single mixture before administering the entire combination through the feeding tube, similar to what the colleague is suggesting"}}
questions.rationale: Best practice for administering multiple medications via a feeding tube includes giving each medication separately, with water flushes between each medication (and before/after the entire process), to prevent potential drug interactions or incompatibilities within the tube and to help maintain tube patency.
questions.source_name: ISMP — Safe Practices for Medication Administration via Enteral Feeding Tubes
questions.source_detail: Sequential Administration and Flushing Technique

questions.stem: A client experiencing respiratory distress is most likely to benefit from which positioning?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A flat, supine position, which would not support the client's current respiratory distress","B":"High-Fowler's position (sitting upright), which allows for maximal lung expansion","C":"A prone position with the head turned to one side, which limits full lung expansion","D":"A Trendelenburg, or head-down, position, which would worsen this client's breathing difficulty"}}
questions.rationale: High-Fowler's position (sitting the client upright, typically at 60-90 degrees) allows for maximal lung expansion by reducing pressure from abdominal organs on the diaphragm and optimizing chest wall movement, making it the preferred position for a client experiencing respiratory distress, unless otherwise contraindicated.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Positioning for Respiratory Distress
questions.source_detail: High-Fowler's Position for Optimal Lung Expansion

questions.stem: A nurse is performing oral suctioning for a client unable to clear their own secretions. Correct technique includes:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Applying continuous suction throughout both insertion and withdrawal, with no set time limit","B":"Inserting the catheter as far as possible while applying continuous suction throughout the pass","C":"Applying intermittent suction primarily during withdrawal, limiting each suction pass to a brief duration, and reassessing the client between passes","D":"Suctioning the client only a single time, regardless of whether secretions continue to be present"}}
questions.rationale: Correct oral suctioning technique involves applying suction intermittently, primarily during catheter withdrawal, limiting each pass to a brief duration to minimize mucosal trauma and hypoxia, and reassessing the client's respiratory status and secretion clearance between passes, repeating as needed.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Oral Suctioning Technique
questions.source_detail: Proper Technique for Oral Suctioning

questions.stem: A nurse needs to change the bed linens for a client who is unable to get out of bed. The nurse should use which technique?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The occupied bed-making technique, working from side to side, rolling the client safely while maintaining privacy, safety, and proper body mechanics","B":"Skip changing the bed linens entirely for any client who is unable to get out of bed independently","C":"Remove all of the linens completely before placing clean ones, leaving the client briefly uncovered","D":"Ask the client to stand briefly during the linen change, regardless of their current mobility status"}}
questions.rationale: For a client unable to get out of bed, the nurse uses the occupied bed-making technique, working from one side of the bed to the other, safely rolling the client (with assistance as needed) while maintaining the client's privacy, safety, comfort, and proper body mechanics for the nurse throughout the process.
questions.source_name: Standard Nursing Fundamentals — Occupied Bed-Making Technique
questions.source_detail: Safe Technique for Changing Linens with a Client in Bed

questions.stem: A nurse is counseling a middle-aged male client about prostate cancer screening (PSA testing), and the client's brother, who was recently diagnosed, insists the client should have started PSA testing years ago at age 18. Current guidance generally recommends instead:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"That PSA testing offers negligible potential value for most clients and is rarely considered clinically appropriate at any age or risk level today, contrary to why screening is being discussed with this client at all","B":"That a single elevated PSA result alone is fully sufficient to confirm a definitive diagnosis of prostate cancer without any additional diagnostic workup, which overstates what a PSA result alone can tell providers","C":"An individualized, shared decision-making discussion with the provider about the potential benefits and harms of PSA screening, typically starting around age 50, earlier with certain risk factors, rather than age 18 as the brother suggested","D":"Beginning routine PSA testing starting at age 18 for most clients, with little regard for family history, race, or other individual risk factors, similar to what the client's brother is currently suggesting"}}
questions.rationale: Current guidance (such as from USPSTF) generally recommends an individualized, shared decision-making approach to PSA screening, discussing potential benefits (early detection) and harms (false positives, overdiagnosis, and treatment-related side effects) with the provider, typically beginning around age 50 for average-risk men, earlier for those with additional risk factors such as family history or being Black.
questions.source_name: USPSTF — Prostate Cancer Screening Recommendations
questions.source_detail: Shared Decision-Making Approach to PSA Screening

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client how to perform a skin self-exam to check moles for potential skin cancer warning signs. The nurse should teach the client the "ABCDE" mnemonic, which includes checking for:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Only the color of a mole, with no attention paid to its shape, size, or overall symmetry","B":"Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter greater than 6mm, and Evolving (changing) characteristics","C":"Only moles that are painful to the touch, with no attention paid to their visual appearance","D":"A mnemonic tool with no established relevance to screening for early signs of skin cancer"}}
questions.rationale: The ABCDE mnemonic for skin self-exams teaches clients to check moles for: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation (multiple colors within one mole), Diameter greater than about 6mm, and Evolving characteristics (any change in size, shape, or color over time) — all warning signs that should prompt further evaluation by a healthcare provider.
questions.source_name: American Academy of Dermatology — ABCDE Rule for Skin Cancer Detection
questions.source_detail: Components of the ABCDE Mnemonic

questions.stem: A nurse is explaining the purpose of routine newborn hearing screening to new parents. The nurse should explain that this screening is important because:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Hearing screening is believed to have no meaningful impact on a child's long-term developmental outcomes","B":"Early identification of hearing loss allows for timely intervention, which supports optimal speech, language, and cognitive development","C":"Hearing loss in infants is considered extremely rare, making routine screening largely unnecessary","D":"Screening is recommended only for infants who already have a known family history of hearing loss"}}
questions.rationale: Routine newborn hearing screening (recommended for all infants, typically before hospital discharge) allows for early identification of hearing loss, which is important because timely intervention (before 6 months of age, when possible) significantly supports optimal speech, language, and cognitive development, given the critical early window for auditory-based learning.
questions.source_name: CDC — Early Hearing Detection and Intervention (EHDI) Program
questions.source_detail: Importance of Early Newborn Hearing Screening

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a client with suspected bulimia nervosa whose weight actually falls within the normal range, leading a colleague to doubt an eating disorder could be present at all given this normal weight. Which finding would actually be most consistent with this condition?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by compensatory behaviors, such as self-induced vomiting, laxative misuse, or excessive exercise, often with a body weight in the normal or above-normal range, addressing the colleague's doubt based on weight alone","B":"A pattern of strict, ongoing caloric restriction with essentially no binge eating episodes, typically resulting in a notably low overall body weight, a pattern more consistent with anorexia than bulimia","C":"A strong preoccupation with body shape paired with infrequent, mild binge episodes occurring mainly during unusually high stress, which understates the recurrent pattern actually seen in bulimia","D":"Significant, sustained restriction of food intake leading to a low body weight, without any recurrent binge eating or purging, a pattern more consistent with anorexia than the bulimia being assessed here"}}
questions.rationale: Bulimia nervosa is characterized by recurrent episodes of binge eating followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors (such as self-induced vomiting, laxative or diuretic misuse, fasting, or excessive exercise) to prevent weight gain, often occurring in individuals with a body weight in the normal or above-normal range, distinct from anorexia nervosa's pattern of restriction and low body weight.
questions.source_name: DSM-5-TR — Diagnostic Criteria for Bulimia Nervosa
questions.source_detail: Core Features of Bulimia Nervosa

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing an adolescent client with a pattern of behavior that includes aggression toward people and animals, destruction of property, and serious violations of rules, though a teacher dismisses this as just typical rebellious teenage behavior. This presentation is most consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A normal developmental phase of adolescence requiring no further clinical evaluation, similar to what the teacher is currently dismissing this behavior as","B":"A finding entirely unrelated to any recognized psychiatric condition or diagnostic category, contrary to what this specific pattern of behavior actually suggests","C":"Conduct disorder, characterized by a persistent pattern of behavior violating the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms, rather than the typical teenage rebellion the teacher dismissed this as","D":"A simple mood disorder with no accompanying behavioral component, which does not fully capture the aggression and rule violations actually being described"}}
questions.rationale: Conduct disorder is characterized by a repetitive, persistent pattern of behavior in which the basic rights of others or major age-appropriate societal norms are violated, including aggression toward people or animals, destruction of property, deceitfulness or theft, and serious rule violations, distinguishing it from typical adolescent behavior variations.
questions.source_name: DSM-5-TR — Diagnostic Criteria for Conduct Disorder
questions.source_detail: Core Features of Conduct Disorder

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing a child with a pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior toward authority figures, and vindictiveness lasting at least 6 months, and a parent assumes this must be the same thing as conduct disorder that a neighbor's child was diagnosed with. This presentation is most consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A temporary emotional reaction to a recent identifiable stressor, generally expected to resolve within a few weeks, which does not match this child's 6-month duration","B":"A childhood diagnosis marked by frequent anger, arguing with parents or teachers, and a spiteful streak lasting at least six months, without the severe rights violations seen in conduct disorder, distinguishing it from what the parent is assuming","C":"Conduct disorder, which additionally involves more serious violations of others' basic rights, such as physical aggression toward people, animals, or deliberate property destruction, unlike what this particular child's presentation actually describes","D":"A primarily physical medical condition entirely unrelated to mood or behavior, which does not fit this child's actual behavioral presentation"}}
questions.rationale: Oppositional defiant disorder is characterized by a persistent pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior toward authority figures, and vindictiveness, lasting at least 6 months. It is distinguished from conduct disorder by the absence of the more severe violations of others' basic rights (such as aggression toward people/animals or serious rule violations) seen in conduct disorder.
questions.source_name: DSM-5-TR — Diagnostic Criteria for Oppositional Defiant Disorder
questions.source_detail: Core Features and Distinction from Conduct Disorder

questions.stem: A nurse is comparing unfractionated heparin and low molecular weight heparin (LMWH), such as enoxaparin, and a student assumes both require the exact same daily PTT monitoring routine. The nurse understands that, unlike unfractionated heparin, LMWH:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Being always administered as a continuous intravenous infusion rather than a subcutaneous injection, which does not describe how LMWH is actually given","B":"Having fairly little meaningful anticoagulant effect once converted from unfractionated to low molecular weight form, contrary to how LMWH actually works","C":"Generally has more predictable pharmacokinetics and does not require routine PTT monitoring for most clients, contrary to the student's assumption that both require the same monitoring","D":"Requiring daily PTT monitoring for every client, without much regard for which type of heparin is prescribed, similar to what the student is currently assuming"}}
questions.rationale: LMWH generally has more predictable pharmacokinetics compared to unfractionated heparin, so routine PTT monitoring is generally not required for most clients (though anti-Xa monitoring may be used in certain situations, such as renal impairment or pregnancy), and it is typically administered via subcutaneous injection rather than continuous IV infusion.
questions.source_name: Clinical Pharmacology Reference — LMWH vs. Unfractionated Heparin
questions.source_detail: Monitoring Differences Between Heparin Types

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client how to self-administer subcutaneous enoxaparin, and the client mentions their friend always rubs the injection site afterward to "help it absorb faster." Correct technique instead includes:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Injecting into the abdominal subcutaneous tissue, avoiding the 2-inch area around the navel, and not massaging the site afterward, contrary to what the client's friend has apparently been doing","B":"Massaging the injection site vigorously immediately after administering the medication, similar to what the client's friend has apparently been doing","C":"Expelling the air bubble from a prefilled syringe before injecting it into the client's abdomen, which is not the correct technique for this particular prefilled formulation","D":"Injecting the medication into a muscle rather than the subcutaneous tissue for faster absorption, contrary to the correct route for this particular medication"}}
questions.rationale: Enoxaparin is injected into the abdominal subcutaneous tissue (avoiding a 2-inch area around the navel), and the site should not be massaged after injection, since massaging can increase bruising/bleeding risk at the site. Prefilled syringes often contain an air bubble intentionally and manufacturer instructions should be followed regarding whether to expel it.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Enoxaparin
questions.source_detail: Subcutaneous Injection Technique

questions.stem: A client using a transdermal fentanyl patch for chronic pain should be taught to avoid which of the following?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Applying the patch only to skin that is clean, dry, and fully intact before securing it in place and","B":"Exposing the patch area to external heat sources (such as heating pads, hot tubs, or saunas), since heat can significantly increase drug absorption and risk of overdose","C":"Rotating the application site with each new patch applied to help prevent local skin irritation","D":"Disposing of used patches safely by folding the adhesive sides together before discarding them which fails to account for the specific risk factors present in this case"}}
questions.rationale: FDA labeling warns that exposing a transdermal fentanyl patch to external heat sources (heating pads, hot tubs, electric blankets, saunas, heated water beds, prolonged direct sunlight, or fever) can significantly increase the rate of fentanyl absorption, leading to potentially fatal overdose. Clients must be taught to avoid heat exposure to the patch area.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Transdermal Fentanyl
questions.source_detail: Warnings: Heat Exposure and Increased Absorption Risk

questions.stem: A nurse is converting a client's pain regimen from morphine to hydromorphone. The nurse should understand that hydromorphone is:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Not classified as an opioid medication at all, unlike morphine and other similar medications","B":"Significantly less potent than morphine on a milligram-for-milligram basis, requiring higher doses","C":"Identical in potency to morphine, requiring no adjustment when converting between the two medications","D":"Significantly more potent than morphine on a milligram-for-milligram basis, requiring careful dose calculation to avoid overdose"}}
questions.rationale: Hydromorphone is significantly more potent than morphine on a milligram-for-milligram basis (opioid conversion references vary but hydromorphone is commonly considered several times more potent than oral morphine). Careful, accurate dose calculation using appropriate equianalgesic conversion tools is essential when switching between these medications to avoid a dangerous overdose.
questions.source_name: Clinical Pain Management References — Opioid Equianalgesic Conversion
questions.source_detail: Relative Potency of Hydromorphone vs. Morphine

questions.stem: A nurse is administering IV acetaminophen to a client who is also receiving other acetaminophen-containing products for pain, and a colleague assumes the IV route is tracked completely separately with no need to add up the other sources. The nurse should recognize the importance of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Ignoring any other sources of acetaminophen, since the IV route is considered entirely separate, similar to what the colleague is currently assuming","B":"Assuming IV acetaminophen carries no established maximum daily dose limit at all for any client, contrary to how this medication actually needs to be tracked","C":"Calculating the client's total daily acetaminophen dose from all sources, including IV, oral, and combination products, to avoid exceeding the maximum safe daily limit, rather than treating the IV route separately as the colleague assumed","D":"Simply doubling the client's usual oral acetaminophen dose since the intravenous route is being used, which is not an appropriate way to approach this combination"}}
questions.rationale: Since acetaminophen toxicity risk is related to total daily dose regardless of route or product source, the nurse must calculate the client's total daily acetaminophen intake from all sources (IV, oral, and any combination products containing acetaminophen) to ensure the maximum safe daily limit is not exceeded, given the serious risk of hepatotoxicity with overdose.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — IV Acetaminophen
questions.source_detail: Total Daily Dose Calculation Across All Acetaminophen Sources

questions.stem: A nurse is counseling a client with a history of cardiovascular disease about the risks of NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, and the client mentions taking it regularly for joint pain without much concern since it's available over the counter. The nurse should explain that NSAIDs carry a boxed warning for:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"No cardiovascular risk associated with this medication for a client with this history, contrary to why this counseling conversation is actually happening","B":"Increased risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, including myocardial infarction and stroke, which is particularly relevant given this client's own cardiovascular history and regular use","C":"A risk limited just to respiratory effects, with fairly little cardiovascular implication, which does not accurately describe this medication's actual boxed warning","D":"Guaranteed prevention of any future heart attack once the client starts this medication, which is essentially the opposite of the actual risk involved"}}
questions.rationale: FDA labeling for NSAIDs (including ibuprofen) includes a boxed warning regarding increased risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, including myocardial infarction and stroke, which can occur even with short-term use, and the risk may increase with duration of use and in clients with existing cardiovascular disease or risk factors.
questions.source_name: FDA — Boxed Warning for NSAIDs
questions.source_detail: Cardiovascular Thrombotic Risk

questions.stem: A client with diabetes is prescribed a short course of prednisone for an inflammatory condition, and the client assumes their usual diabetes medication routine won't need any changes during this course. The nurse should teach the client to instead anticipate:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fairly little effect on the client's blood glucose levels while taking this corticosteroid, contrary to what the client should actually anticipate during this course","B":"A need to stop essentially all of the client's diabetes medications during steroid therapy, which is not the appropriate approach to this combination","C":"Decreased blood glucose levels that would require reducing the client's diabetes medication dose, which is essentially the opposite of what this combination typically causes","D":"Potential increases in blood glucose levels, requiring closer monitoring and possible temporary adjustment of diabetes medications, contrary to the client's assumption that no changes would be needed"}}
questions.rationale: Corticosteroids such as prednisone can significantly increase blood glucose levels through several mechanisms, including increased hepatic glucose production and insulin resistance. Clients with diabetes should be taught to monitor blood glucose more closely during steroid therapy, and temporary adjustment of diabetes medications may be needed in coordination with the provider.
questions.source_name: FDA Prescribing Information — Prednisone
questions.source_detail: Effect on Blood Glucose in Clients with Diabetes

questions.stem: A client newly started on levothyroxine for hypothyroidism has their TSH level checked periodically, and the client wonders why the dose can't just be adjusted based on how they're feeling day to day. The nurse understands that dose titration for this medication is instead:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Completed after a single dose of the medication, with no further adjustment ever needed, contrary to how titration for this medication actually works","B":"Unrelated to any type of laboratory testing throughout the course of this therapy, contrary to the periodic TSH checks this client is actually undergoing","C":"Based solely on the client's symptom improvement, with no laboratory monitoring needed, similar to what the client is currently wondering about","D":"Guided primarily by periodic TSH monitoring, since clinical effects of dose changes take time to manifest, addressing why symptoms alone aren't used as the client was wondering"}}
questions.rationale: Levothyroxine dose titration is guided primarily by periodic TSH monitoring (generally rechecked after about 6-8 weeks following a dose change, since it takes time for TSH to reach a new steady state), along with clinical symptom assessment, allowing for careful, gradual adjustment to the optimal therapeutic dose.
questions.source_name: American Thyroid Association — Hypothyroidism Treatment Guidelines
questions.source_detail: TSH-Guided Levothyroxine Dose Titration

questions.stem: A client taking an atypical antipsychotic medication long-term mentions to the nurse that their only real concern should be watching for any changes in their heart rhythm. The nurse should clarify that this client should instead be monitored periodically for which broader group of adverse effects?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Metabolic effects, including weight gain, dyslipidemia, and hyperglycemia/diabetes risk, representing a broader set of concerns beyond just the cardiac rhythm the client mentioned","B":"Just cardiac rhythm changes, with fairly little other type of ongoing metabolic monitoring needed, similar to what the client is currently assuming","C":"Fairly little ongoing monitoring being recommended for a client taking this medication class, contrary to what long-term use of this medication actually requires","D":"Just changes in visual acuity, with fairly little attention paid to any metabolic parameter, which does not describe the actual monitoring this medication class requires"}}
questions.rationale: Atypical antipsychotics carry a risk of metabolic syndrome-related adverse effects, including significant weight gain, dyslipidemia, and increased risk of hyperglycemia/diabetes. Guidelines recommend baseline and periodic monitoring of weight/BMI, lipid panel, and blood glucose/HbA1c during long-term treatment with these medications.
questions.source_name: American Diabetes Association / APA — Antipsychotic Metabolic Monitoring Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Metabolic Monitoring for Atypical Antipsychotics

questions.stem: A provider prescribes naloxone alongside a new opioid prescription for a client with risk factors for overdose, and the client feels offended, assuming this implies they are suspected of using illicit drugs. This co-prescribing practice actually reflects:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A requirement that is only considered relevant for clients who use illicit, non-prescribed drugs, similar to what the client is currently assuming about why this was prescribed","B":"A practice that is thought to discourage appropriate pain management for clients in genuine need, contrary to the actual purpose behind this co-prescribing approach","C":"A recommended harm-reduction strategy, providing the client or household members with a potentially life-saving reversal agent in case of accidental overdose, rather than implying illicit use as the client assumed","D":"An unnecessary precaution with no supporting evidence base, contrary to why this co-prescribing approach is actually recommended for clients with these particular risk factors"}}
questions.rationale: Co-prescribing naloxone alongside opioid prescriptions for clients with risk factors for overdose (such as high dose, concurrent benzodiazepine use, or history of substance use disorder) is a recommended harm-reduction strategy endorsed by the CDC and FDA, providing the client and household members with a potentially life-saving reversal agent in case of accidental overdose.
questions.source_name: CDC — Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids
questions.source_detail: Naloxone Co-Prescribing for High-Risk Patients

questions.stem: A hospital pharmacy notifies nursing staff of a national shortage of a commonly used medication, and a nurse assumes this means the medication will simply be unavailable with no backup plan until the shortage resolves. The nurse should instead understand that the facility will likely:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Discontinue the medication for every affected client immediately across the board, without first identifying a therapeutically equivalent alternative, similar to the nurse's current assumption","B":"Notify mainly the prescribing physicians of the shortage directly, with nursing staff generally expected to learn of any resulting changes informally over time","C":"Implement a drug shortage management protocol, which may include using alternative medications, conserving supply for priority uses, and providing staff education about changes, rather than simply going without a plan as the nurse assumed","D":"Continue dispensing the medication at its usual established rate until the facility's existing on-hand stock becomes largely depleted, with no other plan in place"}}
questions.rationale: Healthcare facilities typically respond to drug shortages with a structured management protocol, which may include identifying and using appropriate alternative medications, prioritizing remaining supply for the most critical uses, and providing clear staff education about any resulting changes to reduce the risk of errors during the transition.
questions.source_name: ASHP (American Society of Health-System Pharmacists) — Drug Shortage Management Guidelines
questions.source_detail: Facility Response to Medication Shortages

questions.stem: A nurse notices that two different medications have very similar packaging in the medication storage area, and a colleague shrugs it off since neither has caused a problem yet. This scenario represents a risk factor for:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A situation with fairly little established relevance to overall patient safety on the nursing unit, similar to what the colleague is currently assuming by shrugging it off","B":"A problem that just the pharmacy department needs to address, with fairly little nursing role involved, contrary to the role the nurse who noticed this actually has here","C":"An improvement in overall medication safety, with no concern raised by this type of packaging, contrary to the actual risk this similarity poses","D":"A medication error due to look-alike packaging, warranting a safety report and consideration of storage/labeling changes, rather than shrugging it off as the colleague suggested"}}
questions.rationale: Look-alike packaging is a recognized medication error risk factor. When identified, the nurse should report this safety concern through appropriate channels (such as an incident report or direct communication with pharmacy/safety committee), which may lead to changes such as physical separation of the products, distinct labeling, or other risk-reduction strategies.
questions.source_name: ISMP — Look-Alike Packaging and Labeling Safety Concerns
questions.source_detail: Nursing Role in Identifying Packaging-Related Risks

questions.stem: A hospital uses barcode medication administration (BCMA) technology. The primary purpose of this system is to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Designed to serve as a full substitute for the nurse's own independent double-check of high-alert medications during the administration process itself","B":"Verify the \"rights\" of medication administration electronically (right patient, right medication, right dose, right route, right time) by scanning barcodes, reducing the risk of errors","C":"Limited in scope mainly to scheduled controlled substances specifically, with routine, non-controlled medications instead verified through a separate manual process","D":"Intended mainly as a documentation and billing tool for the facility, with medication error prevention considered a secondary benefit of the system"}}
questions.rationale: Barcode medication administration (BCMA) technology verifies key elements of safe medication administration (such as the correct patient and medication) by scanning barcodes on the client's ID band and the medication packaging, cross-referencing against the electronic medication administration record, helping reduce the risk of medication errors, though it does not replace nursing clinical judgment.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission / ISMP — Barcode Medication Administration Safety Benefits
questions.source_detail: Purpose and Function of BCMA Technology

questions.stem: A nurse is removing IV tubing from an infusion pump, and a colleague assumes this particular safety mechanism is mostly outdated and unnecessary in modern pumps. The nurse should ensure the tubing has a "free-flow protection" mechanism because:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"It is considered a largely redundant safeguard in most modern pumps, since gravity alone rarely delivers a clinically significant volume of fluid, similar to what the colleague is currently assuming","B":"It is relevant chiefly for oral liquid medications delivered through a separate feeding tube system, rather than for IV infusion lines specifically","C":"Without this protection, removing tubing from the pump can result in uncontrolled, rapid infusion of the remaining fluid/medication, posing a serious safety risk, contrary to the colleague's assumption that this safeguard is largely unnecessary","D":"It is designed mainly to slow, rather than fully prevent, uncontrolled flow once the tubing set is removed from the infusion pump"}}
questions.rationale: Free-flow protection is a safety mechanism built into IV tubing/pump systems that prevents uncontrolled, rapid ("free-flow") infusion of fluid or medication when tubing is removed from the pump. Without this protection, a dangerous, unregulated bolus of fluid or medication could be delivered to the client, posing a serious safety risk, particularly with high-alert medications.
questions.source_name: ISMP / FDA — IV Infusion Pump Safety, Free-Flow Protection
questions.source_detail: Purpose of Free-Flow Protection Mechanisms

questions.stem: A nurse adjusts a cardiac monitor's alarm parameters for a specific client based on their baseline vital signs and clinical condition, and a colleague assumes this task is reserved strictly for biomedical engineering staff rather than bedside nurses. This practice actually reflects:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A task generally reserved for biomedical engineering staff, since bedside nurses are not typically trained to adjust cardiac alarm limits, similar to what the colleague is currently assuming","B":"A practice generally discouraged under current guidelines, due to concern that individualized limits could delay recognition of deterioration","C":"Individualized alarm management, which helps ensure alarms are clinically meaningful for that specific client, reducing alarm fatigue while maintaining safety, rather than being reserved for engineering staff as the colleague assumed","D":"An unwarranted deviation from standard factory-set alarm parameters that should be reserved only for critical care units specifically"}}
questions.rationale: Individualizing alarm parameters based on a specific client's baseline and clinical condition (within appropriate, safe limits and per facility policy) helps ensure alarms are clinically meaningful for that client, which can help reduce alarm fatigue from non-actionable alarms while still maintaining an appropriate safety margin — an approach supported by national patient safety goals on alarm management.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — National Patient Safety Goals: Alarm Safety
questions.source_detail: Individualized Alarm Parameter Setting

questions.stem: A hospital's infection prevention team investigates a cluster of similar infections occurring on one unit, and a staff member assumes this cluster is probably just a coincidence not worth digging into further. Which step is instead a core component of this outbreak investigation?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Immediately closing the entire hospital to new admissions with no further investigation, which overstates the appropriate initial response here","B":"Assuming fairly little action is needed until the identified outbreak worsens significantly, similar to what the staff member is currently assuming","C":"Largely ignoring the observed pattern, assuming the cluster of cases is purely coincidental, similar to what the staff member is currently assuming","D":"Systematically identifying cases, analyzing common exposures or risk factors, and implementing targeted control measures based on findings, rather than dismissing the pattern as coincidental as the staff member suggested"}}
questions.rationale: A systematic outbreak investigation involves identifying and characterizing cases, analyzing common exposures, timing, or risk factors to identify a likely source or transmission route, and implementing targeted control measures based on these findings, an epidemiological approach used by infection prevention teams to control and prevent further spread.
questions.source_name: CDC — Outbreak Investigation Principles in Healthcare Settings
questions.source_detail: Core Steps of a Healthcare-Associated Outbreak Investigation

questions.stem: A hospital requires staff to demonstrate competency in proper PPE donning and doffing technique through periodic hands-on training and validation, and a veteran staff member questions why this is needed since they already know how to put gloves and a gown on. This practice is important because:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Proper PPE technique being thought to be intuitive and requiring fairly little formal training, similar to what the veteran staff member is currently assuming","B":"Improper PPE technique, even with correct equipment, can result in self-contamination and increased infection transmission risk, contrary to the veteran staff member's assumption that this training is unnecessary","C":"PPE competency being believed to have fairly little meaningful bearing on overall infection control outcomes, similar to what the veteran staff member is currently assuming","D":"This type of competency training being considered relevant just during an active disease outbreak, contrary to why this training is actually conducted on an ongoing basis"}}
questions.rationale: Even with the correct PPE available, improper donning or doffing technique can result in self-contamination (such as touching a contaminated surface with bare skin during glove/gown removal), increasing infection transmission risk. Periodic hands-on training and competency validation help ensure staff can correctly and consistently perform these critical safety procedures.
questions.source_name: CDC — PPE Training and Competency Validation Guidance
questions.source_detail: Importance of Proper PPE Technique Training

questions.stem: A nurse uses a reusable blood pressure cuff and stethoscope between different clients. Appropriate infection control practice requires:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Sharing the equipment between clients with no cleaning performed if they appear generally healthy","B":"No cleaning at all is needed for reusable equipment shared between different clients","C":"Cleaning/disinfecting the equipment between each client use, per facility protocol, to prevent cross-contamination","D":"Cleaning the shared equipment only once per week, regardless of how frequently it is used"}}
questions.rationale: Reusable, non-critical medical equipment (such as blood pressure cuffs and stethoscopes) that contacts intact skin should be cleaned/disinfected between each client use, per facility protocol, to prevent cross-contamination and transmission of pathogens between clients, since equipment can serve as a fomite for transmission if not properly cleaned.
questions.source_name: CDC — Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization, Noncritical Equipment
questions.source_detail: Cleaning Requirements for Reusable Equipment Between Patients

questions.stem: A nurse consults the ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses when facing an ethical dilemma in practice. This document is best described as:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A foundational document outlining the ethical obligations and values central to the nursing profession, guiding professional conduct","B":"A document relevant only to nursing students, with no ongoing relevance to practicing nurses","C":"A legal statute carrying the direct force of law in every single U.S. state","D":"An entirely optional set of suggestions carrying no genuine professional significance"}}
questions.rationale: The ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses is a foundational document outlining the ethical obligations, values, and professional conduct standards central to the nursing profession. While not itself a law, it is widely recognized as an authoritative standard for professional nursing practice and ethical decision-making.
questions.source_name: ANA — Code of Ethics for Nurses with Interpretive Statements
questions.source_detail: Purpose and Significance of the Code of Ethics

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client who also happens to be a personal friend outside of work, and the nurse initially assumes this pre-existing friendship poses no real professional complication as long as care is provided competently. This situation illustrates the concept of:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A scenario that carries no potential for ethical complexity in this type of situation, similar to what the nurse is currently assuming","B":"A dual relationship, which requires careful attention to maintaining appropriate professional boundaries despite the pre-existing personal relationship, contrary to the nurse's initial assumption that there's no real complication here","C":"A situation with fairly little meaningful professional relevance to the nurse's ongoing practice, similar to what the nurse is currently assuming","D":"A situation that generally requires immediate reassignment with fairly little other option considered, which overstates the appropriate response to this kind of dual relationship"}}
questions.rationale: A dual relationship occurs when a nurse has both a professional and a pre-existing personal relationship (such as friendship or family) with a client, which requires careful, thoughtful attention to maintaining appropriate professional boundaries and objectivity, and in some cases may warrant discussion with a supervisor about the most appropriate way to proceed.
questions.source_name: NCSBN — Professional Boundaries Guidelines, Dual Relationships
questions.source_detail: Navigating Dual Relationships in Nursing Practice

questions.stem: A nurse licensed in a state that is not part of the Nurse Licensure Compact wants to work temporarily in another state, and assumes the current license will simply carry over automatically since nursing standards are fairly similar everywhere. The nurse should instead understand that:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"They can begin practicing immediately in the new state under a temporary grace period that most individual state boards are presumed to formally and automatically recognize, similar to what the nurse is currently assuming","B":"No nursing license is required at all in the new state, provided the work performed there is limited to a fairly short-term temporary assignment","C":"Licensure requirements are considered largely interchangeable across state lines, since most boards are presumed to recognize one another's standards, similar to the nurse's current assumption","D":"They will generally need to obtain licensure (or an appropriate temporary permit) in the new state, since a non-compact license is not automatically portable, contrary to what the nurse is currently assuming"}}
questions.rationale: Outside of Nurse Licensure Compact arrangements, nursing licensure is generally state-specific, meaning a nurse licensed in a non-compact state (or seeking to practice in a state outside compact recognition) will typically need to obtain licensure or an appropriate temporary permit in the state where they intend to practice, since licenses are not automatically portable without such agreements.
questions.source_name: NCSBN — State Licensure and Nurse Licensure Compact
questions.source_detail: Licensure Requirements Outside Compact Arrangements

questions.stem: A new nurse asks about the value of carrying individual professional liability insurance separate from employer coverage, assuming the employer's policy would fully protect them in any situation they could realistically face at work. The nurse educator should explain that individual coverage:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Is largely redundant in most typical cases, since employer coverage is assumed to extend to cover any situation, similar to what the new nurse is currently assuming","B":"Can provide additional protection, since employer coverage may prioritize the employer's interests and may not cover all situations, such as actions outside the scope of employment","C":"Is restricted under most current state regulations, which are presumed to broadly limit individual nurses from purchasing coverage outside their employer's plan","D":"Would offer only negligible added protection beyond what a typical employer policy already provides, similar to what the new nurse is currently assuming"}}
questions.rationale: While many employers provide some liability coverage, individual professional liability insurance can offer additional protection, since employer-provided coverage may primarily prioritize the employer's interests in a dispute and may not extend to situations outside the nurse's direct employment (such as Good Samaritan situations, volunteer work, or if the nurse's and employer's interests diverge in a claim).
questions.source_name: ANA — Considerations for Individual Professional Liability Insurance
questions.source_detail: Value of Individual Malpractice Coverage

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a client involved in a legal case requiring collection of forensic evidence, such as during a sexual assault examination, and a newer colleague assumes the nurse's responsibility ends the moment the evidence is collected. Maintaining proper "chain of custody" is important because:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"It is handled exclusively by law enforcement personnel once evidence leaves the facility, with the nurse's documented role ending at collection, similar to what the newer colleague is currently assuming","B":"It is relevant mainly when evidence happens to be collected in a non-clinical setting, rather than during a hospital-based forensic examination like this one","C":"It documents the handling of evidence from collection through final disposition, helping ensure its integrity and admissibility in legal proceedings","D":"It is primarily a documentation formality with limited practical bearing on whether the evidence is later accepted as admissible in court"}}
questions.rationale: Chain of custody refers to the documented, unbroken record of evidence handling from the moment of collection through its final disposition (such as transfer to law enforcement), which helps ensure the evidence's integrity and admissibility in legal proceedings. Nurses involved in forensic evidence collection (such as SANE — Sexual Assault Nurse Examiners) play a critical role in maintaining proper chain of custody.
questions.source_name: International Association of Forensic Nurses — Chain of Custody Standards
questions.source_detail: Nursing Role in Maintaining Chain of Custody

questions.stem: A sentinel event occurs at a hospital accredited by The Joint Commission, and a staff member assumes the organization can simply address it internally on its own timeline with no external reporting requirement. The organization is instead generally expected to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Conduct a thorough root cause analysis and submit required documentation within a specific timeframe defined by Joint Commission sentinel event policy","B":"Wait indefinitely, with fairly little specific timeframe expectation for the organization's formal response to this kind of event","C":"Only report the sentinel event if specifically requested to do so by an outside party sometime after the fact occurs","D":"Take fairly little further action, since reporting the event is largely considered an optional step for the organization"}}
questions.rationale: Per The Joint Commission's Sentinel Event Policy, accredited organizations are generally expected to conduct a thorough, credible root cause analysis and submit required documentation within a specific timeframe (historically within 45 business days of the event or of becoming aware of it, though organizations should verify current specific requirements), reflecting the seriousness and priority given to sentinel event response.
questions.source_name: The Joint Commission — Sentinel Event Policy
questions.source_detail: Expected Timeframe for Root Cause Analysis Submission

questions.stem: A serious medical error occurs, resulting in harm to a client, and the care team plans to disclose the error to the client's family. A team member suggests one person should just handle the whole conversation alone without looping in any other department. Best practice for this disclosure conversation instead includes:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Assigning the entire disclosure conversation to a single team member alone, without broader organizational involvement or risk management support, similar to what the team member is currently suggesting","B":"Honest, timely, compassionate communication about what happened, expressing empathy and outlining next steps, ideally involving risk management support","C":"Limiting expressions of empathy during the conversation, out of concern that empathy could be misinterpreted later as an admission of fault","D":"Postponing the disclosure conversation indefinitely until any related legal proceedings have been fully resolved through the court system"}}
questions.rationale: Best practice for disclosing a serious medical error to a client/family includes honest, timely, and compassionate communication about what happened, genuine expression of empathy and concern (which does not equate to a legal admission of fault, though language should still be handled thoughtfully), and outlining next steps — ideally with support from risk management, patient relations, or other institutional resources experienced in disclosure conversations.
questions.source_name: IHI / The Joint Commission — Communication and Resolution After Adverse Events
questions.source_detail: Best Practices for Error Disclosure Conversations

questions.stem: A nurse is providing discharge teaching and wants to ensure the client truly understands the instructions, given concerns about the client's health literacy. An effective technique is to:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Simply asking the client, 'Do you understand?' and accepting a yes or no answer as sufficient","B":"Providing only written discharge materials, with no accompanying verbal discussion at all","C":"Use the \"teach-back\" method, asking the client to explain the instructions in their own words to confirm understanding","D":"Assuming the client understands based solely on their level of formal education"}}
questions.rationale: The "teach-back" method — asking the client to explain instructions or demonstrate a skill in their own words — is a recommended, evidence-based technique to confirm true understanding, since simply asking "Do you understand?" often yields an inaccurate yes/no response that does not reliably indicate comprehension, particularly important for clients with limited health literacy.
questions.source_name: AHRQ — Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit, Teach-Back Method
questions.source_detail: Using Teach-Back to Confirm Client Understanding

questions.stem: A nurse is distinguishing between septic shock and cardiogenic shock in a hypotensive client. The nurse understands that septic shock, unlike cardiogenic shock, is typically characterized by:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Cool, clammy skin along with an elevated systemic vascular resistance in the early phase","B":"Identical hemodynamic findings occurring in both septic shock and cardiogenic shock","C":"A complete absence of any skin color or temperature changes in either type of shock","D":"Warm, flushed skin (in the early/warm phase) due to widespread vasodilation and decreased systemic vascular resistance"}}
questions.rationale: In the early ("warm") phase of septic shock, widespread vasodilation from the inflammatory response leads to warm, flushed skin and decreased systemic vascular resistance, contrasting with cardiogenic shock, which typically presents with cool, clammy skin and elevated systemic vascular resistance due to compensatory vasoconstriction in response to poor cardiac output.
questions.source_name: Society of Critical Care Medicine — Shock Classification and Hemodynamic Profiles
questions.source_detail: Distinguishing Septic from Cardiogenic Shock

questions.stem: A client with heart failure develops sudden severe dyspnea, pink frothy sputum, and crackles throughout both lung fields, and a family member assumes this is just the client's usual heart failure symptoms acting up a bit. The nurse should instead recognize this as consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"A simple upper respiratory infection, a diagnosis inconsistent with this particular presentation and its severity","B":"Expected heart failure symptoms requiring no escalation of care, similar to what the family member is currently assuming about this presentation","C":"A normal finding in this client requiring no urgent nursing action, contrary to the severity of what is actually being described here","D":"Acute pulmonary edema, a medical emergency requiring immediate intervention, rather than the usual symptom pattern the family member assumed"}}
questions.rationale: Sudden severe dyspnea, pink frothy sputum, and diffuse crackles are classic signs of acute pulmonary edema, a life-threatening complication of heart failure (or other causes) in which fluid accumulates in the alveoli, requiring immediate intervention, including oxygen, positioning (upright), and prompt provider notification for further emergency treatment.
questions.source_name: American Heart Association — Acute Pulmonary Edema Recognition and Management
questions.source_detail: Clinical Presentation of Acute Pulmonary Edema

questions.stem: A client with severe, long-standing COPD develops signs of right-sided heart failure, including peripheral edema and jugular venous distention, and a new nurse assumes these findings must point to a separate, unrelated kidney problem. The nurse should instead recognize this as consistent with:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Left-sided heart failure exclusively, a diagnosis inconsistent with this particular client's presentation and the right-sided findings described","B":"An unrelated renal condition, similar to what the new nurse is currently assuming, rather than a condition connected to the client's COPD","C":"Cor pulmonale, right-sided heart failure resulting from chronic pulmonary disease, rather than the unrelated kidney issue the new nurse assumed","D":"A normal finding entirely unrelated to the client's long-standing underlying lung disease, contrary to what these findings actually reflect"}}
questions.rationale: Cor pulmonale refers to right-sided heart failure resulting from chronic pulmonary disease (such as severe COPD), in which increased pulmonary vascular resistance from lung disease places excessive strain on the right ventricle over time, eventually leading to signs of right-sided heart failure such as peripheral edema and jugular venous distention.
questions.source_name: American Thoracic Society — Cor Pulmonale in Chronic Lung Disease
questions.source_detail: Pathophysiology and Recognition of Cor Pulmonale

questions.stem: A client reports progressive dyspnea and dull, decreased breath sounds on one side of the chest, and a colleague assumes this is probably just an unrelated abdominal issue causing referred discomfort. The nurse should instead suspect:
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"An unrelated abdominal condition, similar to what the colleague is currently assuming, rather than a condition affecting the chest itself","B":"A pleural effusion, warranting further evaluation such as a chest X-ray, rather than the abdominal cause the colleague assumed","C":"A simple muscle strain, a diagnosis inconsistent with this particular unilateral breath sound finding and progressive dyspnea","D":"A normal finding in this client requiring no further diagnostic evaluation, contrary to what this asymmetric finding actually suggests"}}
questions.rationale: Progressive dyspnea with dull percussion and decreased or absent breath sounds over an area of the chest are classic findings of a pleural effusion (fluid accumulation in the pleural space), warranting further evaluation, such as chest X-ray or ultrasound, to confirm and guide management, potentially including thoracentesis.
questions.source_name: American Thoracic Society — Pleural Effusion Clinical Presentation
questions.source_detail: Classic Findings of Pleural Effusion
